title: Former AARO Head Says Lockheed Crashed Saucer Claims Come from UFO Profiteers
excerpt: ​The former head of the Pentagon’s UFO investigation arm said in a recent interview that recent claims Lockheed Martin houses a dozen alien spaceships aren’t just false—they were also...
content:
​The former head of the Pentagon’s UFO investigation arm said in a recent interview that recent claims Lockheed Martin houses a dozen alien spaceships aren’t just false—they were also promoted by a group of grifters looking to direct millions of dollars toward UFO enthusiasts with close ties to powerful people. Sean Kirkpatrick, who led AARO until 2023, told Paradigm’s Ben Schreckinger that the claims circulating around Lockheed’s deceased vice president Jim Ryder could not be substantiated. In his recent memoir, Jay Stratton, who headed an earlier Pentagon UFO investigation, alleged that Ryder had told him about a vast eighty-year conspiracy involving hundreds of UFO crashes and dozens of flying saucers kept in storage. Kirkpatrick said that there was no evidence that Ryder had said or done any of the things attributed to him; instead, the stories appear to be the work of UFO disclosure advocates.

​Kirkpatrick added that he sought to find the alleged Lockheed UFOs but determined the story was false. “As for the Lockheed allegations, I investigated that with Lockheed’s Chief Tech Officer and found it [to] be connected with people who had both misled the company and were trying to make money on aerospace tech unconnected to aliens,” he wrote in an email to Schreckinger. “It is convenient that these stories and allegations always involve someone who knew it all but has died.”

Kirkpatrick told Steven Greenstreet of the New York Post that the people misleading Lockheed and the government were affiliated with To the Stars Academy of Arts and Science, the Tom Delonge-led UFO organization made up of ex-government UFO investigators such as Hal Puthoff and (at one time) Lue Elizondo.

 As I reported last week, the allegation about Lockheed’s fleet of captured flying saucers is a very recent one, only tracing back in the public record a few years. I said at the time that it appeared to have originated in lore created by and spread among government UFO investigators.   

 Kirkpatrick added that staffers for members of Congress with a special interest in UFOs attempted to order Kirkpatrick to give millions of dollars in funding to the same UFO advocates who were perpetrating the false claims about Lockheed. “There were the earmarks that they tried to get Congress to put in to direct me to funnel money to these people to ‘investigate’ UAP,” Kirkpatrick told Schreckinger. “I had one staffer call me up and direct me to send several million dollars.” He added that the money stayed put after Kirkpatrick asked for the request in writing so it could go through an official legal review. No one wanted to put it on paper.
